title: The Favoured Applicant
question: A recruiter likes one applicant's opening story and spends the interview seeking examples of initiative. Other applicants get tougher questions about failures. Which redesign best tests whether the first impression is deserved?
choices: Score identical work samples before conducting any interviews
Give every applicant more time to describe personal strengths
Ask a second recruiter whether the opening story sounded credible
Let the recruiter add more evidence supporting the early impression
correctAnswer: Score identical work samples before conducting any interviews
correctExplanation: Exactly. A common task gathered before personal contact prevents an early preference from deciding which evidence gets requested and noticed.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the strongest fix is to score identical work samples before conducting any interviews. More conversation can simply produce more selectively gathered support; standardization creates comparable evidence before a favourite exists.
lessonContent:
Confirmation bias changes which questions we ask, not only how we judge the answers.
Early impressions are especially powerful when later evidence is gathered selectively.
Standardized evidence makes candidates comparable instead of letting each conversation follow its own theory.
Separating evidence collection from judgement reduces opportunities to protect a first guess.
Share this: write three fixed questions before your next interview or important conversation.

title: The Brilliant Seller
question: A salesperson exceeds every target, so executives assume she will also coach patiently, plan budgets well, and resolve conflict. What is the best response before promoting her to management?
choices: Treat exceptional sales as proof of broad professional excellence
Assess coaching, budgeting, and conflict skills as separate competencies
Ask her best clients whether they admire her personality
Promote her temporarily because success usually transfers across roles
correctAnswer: Assess coaching, budgeting, and conflict skills as separate competencies
correctExplanation: Right. Sales performance is relevant evidence about selling, not automatic evidence about unrelated management skills; each trait needs its own test.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, assess coaching, budgeting, and conflict skills as separate competencies. The halo from one conspicuous strength makes unmeasured traits feel proven, while admiration and temporary promotion preserve the same inference.
lessonContent:
A halo forms when one vivid strength spills into ratings of unrelated qualities.
Role changes are risky because excellence in the old task can hide missing skills in the new one.
Independent scorecards force each competency to earn its own evidence.
Specific behavioural tests beat global impressions such as 'leadership material.'
Share this: split one broad judgement of a colleague into three separately evidenced traits.

title: Tutorial Confidence
question: After one coding tutorial, Mina says she is ready to secure a payment system because every exercise felt easy. Which check most directly tests whether her confidence has outrun her competence?
choices: Ask how motivated she felt while completing the tutorial
Let her explain why the examples seemed straightforward
Give her unfamiliar security tasks with expert-scored failure cases
Count how many tutorial sections she completed without pausing
correctAnswer: Give her unfamiliar security tasks with expert-scored failure cases
correctExplanation: Exactly. Transfer to unfamiliar tasks and expert evaluation reveal blind spots that guided exercises conceal.
incorrectExplanation: Close! The answer is to give her unfamiliar security tasks with expert-scored failure cases. Ease inside a guided tutorial may measure scaffolding, while independent transfer exposes whether she can recognize and handle errors herself.
lessonContent:
Beginners can mistake fluency with examples for mastery of a domain.
Metacognition depends partly on the same knowledge needed to perform the task.
Novel problems reveal whether learning transfers beyond the training format.
External criteria calibrate confidence more reliably than feelings of ease.
Share this: test one newly learned skill on an unfamiliar problem before claiming mastery.

title: The Miracle Thread
question: Leo believes a supplement improves memory. He collects dozens of enthusiastic posts from users who felt sharper. Which missing evidence would most challenge his conclusion?
choices: Whether the posts use scientific-sounding vocabulary
Whether some users took the supplement for several months
Whether the most enthusiastic users recommend the same brand
Whether comparable non-users improved, and how many users noticed nothing
correctAnswer: Whether comparable non-users improved, and how many users noticed nothing
correctExplanation: Correct. Testimonials omit both a comparison group and the silent failures, so they cannot show that the supplement caused improvement.
incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: ask whether comparable non-users improved, and how many users noticed nothing. Supporting stories are selected from visible successes; a denominator and comparison group test the belief rather than decorate it.
lessonContent:
Evidence selected by satisfied users hides failures and natural improvement.
A denominator asks how many total cases produced the celebrated successes.
A comparison group estimates what would have happened without the intervention.
Good belief testing searches for missing cases, not merely additional stories.
Share this: ask 'out of how many?' the next time a testimonial impresses you.

title: Luxury in a Glass
question: Guests rate wine from an elegant heavy bottle as richer than the same wine poured from a plain bottle. Which follow-up best isolates the wine's actual sensory quality?
choices: Serve coded samples under identical conditions and compare ratings
Tell guests that both bottles came from respected vineyards
Invite experienced collectors to inspect both labels closely
Repeat the tasting after displaying the premium bottle longer
correctAnswer: Serve coded samples under identical conditions and compare ratings
correctExplanation: Exactly. Blind, matched presentation removes the packaging glow, leaving the liquid as the meaningful difference.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to serve coded samples under identical conditions and compare ratings. Prestige cues can spread into taste judgements; more label information or exposure strengthens that halo instead of isolating sensory evidence.
lessonContent:
Status cues can colour perception before the underlying object is evaluated.
Branding, price, and presentation often act as halos around identical products.
Blinding removes identity cues that could leak into supposedly independent ratings.
Matched conditions ensure that only the feature under study changes.
Share this: compare two everyday products once without seeing their brands.

title: Borrowed Expertise
question: A celebrated architect insists he can personally audit the firm's cybersecurity because he solves complex design problems daily. What should the partners infer?
choices: Complex expertise reliably transfers to any other complex domain
His cybersecurity judgement needs the same external validation as a novice's
His confidence proves he has learned enough informally to lead the audit
Architectural success makes technical mistakes unlikely in general
correctAnswer: His cybersecurity judgement needs the same external validation as a novice's
correctExplanation: Right. Expertise is domain-specific; distinction in architecture does not supply the concepts needed to detect one's cybersecurity errors.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — his cybersecurity judgement needs the same external validation as a novice's. General intelligence may help learning, but it does not replace domain knowledge or make self-assessment accurate in a new field.
lessonContent:
Expertise usually consists of domain-specific patterns, feedback, and error knowledge.
Success in one difficult field can create unjustified confidence in another.
General intelligence accelerates learning but does not erase novice blind spots.
Calibration requires tests tied to the domain being claimed.
Share this: name one area where your professional confidence should not automatically transfer.

title: The Favourite Bug
question: A developer thinks a memory leak causes an app crash. Logs showing rising memory excite her; stable-memory crashes get called 'noise.' What is the most informative next test?
choices: Collect more examples in which memory rises before a crash
Ask teammates why memory leaks often cause instability
Predict an observation the leak theory forbids, then try to produce it
Rewrite the logs so memory changes appear more prominently
correctAnswer: Predict an observation the leak theory forbids, then try to produce it
correctExplanation: Exactly. A risky prediction creates a chance for the theory to fail, unlike collecting more compatible cases.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, predict an observation the leak theory forbids, then try to produce it. A hypothesis gains diagnostic value from surviving possible refutation; supportive examples alone may fit many competing causes.
lessonContent:
Confirmation testing asks whether evidence fits; falsification asks what the idea cannot survive.
A useful hypothesis excludes some possible observations.
Anomalies should update a theory rather than be relabelled automatically as noise.
Competing explanations become clearer when each makes a different prediction.
Share this: write one result that would disprove your current explanation of a problem.

title: The Famous Face
question: A beloved actor fronts a disaster charity. Donations surge because supporters assume a kind public persona means the organization is effective. What is the most relevant check?
choices: How consistently the actor has played sympathetic characters
How warmly audiences describe the actor in interviews
How many other celebrities praise the campaign publicly
How independently audited outcomes compare with similar charities
correctAnswer: How independently audited outcomes compare with similar charities
correctExplanation: Correct. The actor's likability is separate from the charity's cost, governance, and measured impact.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to check how independently audited outcomes compare with similar charities. Celebrity warmth can illuminate unrelated judgements, while comparative outcome evidence evaluates the organization itself.
lessonContent:
Admiration for a messenger can spread to claims and organizations they endorse.
A trustworthy evaluation follows money and outcomes rather than borrowed affection.
Independent audits reduce the influence of reputation on measurement.
Comparisons matter because a good intention may still produce weak results.
Share this: check one endorsed cause by its measured impact rather than its spokesperson.

title: The Lucky Trade
question: Noah makes one risky stock pick after watching two videos; it doubles, and he concludes he can beat professional investors. Which evaluation best separates skill from luck?
choices: Track many pre-recorded decisions against a suitable benchmark
Measure how strongly Noah now believes in his investing method
Compare his profit with friends who avoided that particular stock
Ask whether he can tell a persuasive story about the winning company
correctAnswer: Track many pre-recorded decisions against a suitable benchmark
correctExplanation: Exactly. A long, recorded sample compared with a benchmark can reveal repeatable advantage; one noisy win cannot.
incorrectExplanation: Close! Track many pre-recorded decisions against a suitable benchmark. Confidence and a compelling story are compatible with luck, while repeated out-of-sample performance tests whether the claimed skill persists.
lessonContent:
Noisy domains can reward weak methods over short runs.
A lucky outcome often raises confidence faster than it raises competence.
Pre-recording prevents winners from quietly forgetting their losing predictions.
Benchmarks show whether performance exceeds what ordinary exposure would produce.
Share this: keep a dated scorecard for your next ten predictions in a noisy domain.

title: The Friendly Feed
question: Priya's news feed mostly shows articulate arguments for her political view. She wants to know whether the view survives serious challenge, not merely whether supporters can defend it. What should she do?
choices: Read a larger number of posts recommended by the same feed
Seek the strongest opposing case and state it fairly before replying
Count how many supportive posts include links to any source
Mute emotional supporters while retaining only calm supporters
correctAnswer: Seek the strongest opposing case and state it fairly before replying
correctExplanation: Right. A strong opposing case probes the belief's weakest points; more polished agreement only deepens the same evidence channel.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — seek the strongest opposing case and state it fairly before replying. Filtering for calmer allies may improve tone but not exposure to disconfirming reasons; fair restatement prevents dismissing a caricature.
lessonContent:
Selective exposure can make a contested belief feel unanimously supported.
Algorithms learn engagement preferences, not which evidence a belief most needs.
Steel-manning means reconstructing the strongest rival case before evaluating it.
A view tested against weak opponents has not yet passed a serious test.
Share this: summarize one opposing argument so its advocate would say you got it right.

title: One Late Report
question: An employee with years of strong work misses one visible deadline. Her manager now describes her ideas, communication, and judgement as generally poor. Which correction best prevents one failure from darkening every score?
choices: Delay the review until the missed deadline feels less irritating
Ask colleagues whether they were also disappointed by the delay
Rate each competency from its own behavioural record and time window
Average the manager's overall impression with the employee's self-rating
correctAnswer: Rate each competency from its own behavioural record and time window
correctExplanation: Exactly. Trait-specific evidence prevents a salient failure from becoming a negative halo over unrelated performance.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to rate each competency from its own behavioural record and time window. Waiting may cool emotion, but only separate evidence stops one event from contaminating every category.
lessonContent:
Negative halos are often called horn effects: one flaw darkens unrelated ratings.
Recent, vivid failures can outweigh a long and relevant record.
Behaviourally anchored scales force vague impressions into observable evidence.
Separate time windows keep one incident from rewriting an entire history.
Share this: revisit one global criticism and identify the exact behaviour it actually supports.

title: The Expert Shortcut
question: A veteran analyst says a new dashboard is intuitive and needs no instructions. New hires repeatedly fail to use it. Which evidence would best reveal whether expertise is hiding the design's difficulty?
choices: The analyst's speed after years of using similar dashboards
A vote among the experienced designers who built the interface
The number of advanced features available to expert users
Observed first-time users completing realistic tasks without coaching
correctAnswer: Observed first-time users completing realistic tasks without coaching
correctExplanation: Correct. Novice task performance tests the interface for its intended learners; expert ease may reflect knowledge they no longer notice using.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is observed first-time users completing realistic tasks without coaching. Experienced designers share hidden assumptions, so their confidence cannot substitute for watching the target users work independently.
lessonContent:
Deep skill can make experts underestimate how many steps beginners must learn.
Automatic knowledge becomes hard to notice and therefore hard to explain.
Usability must be measured with representative users, not only creators.
Watching unaided performance exposes instructions that experts silently supply themselves.
Share this: ask a beginner to try something you designed while you remain silent.

title: The Ominous Text
question: After suspecting a friend is angry, Sam reads 'fine, talk later' as hostile and remembers only curt replies. Which move best checks the suspicion without simply seeking reassurance?
choices: List rival explanations and specify what each predicts next
Reread every short message until its hostile tone feels clearer
Ask another worried friend whether the wording also seems cold
Collect earlier occasions when brief replies preceded an argument
correctAnswer: List rival explanations and specify what each predicts next
correctExplanation: Exactly. Competing explanations turn an ambiguous cue into testable predictions instead of allowing suspicion to interpret every detail.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, list rival explanations and specify what each predicts next. Repeated reading and like-minded consultation can strengthen the original frame; distinct predictions create evidence capable of separating anger from busyness or fatigue.
lessonContent:
Ambiguous evidence readily takes the shape of an existing expectation.
Generating alternatives interrupts the jump from cue to single story.
Predictions make explanations compete on future evidence rather than emotional fit.
Memory search is biased when only one theory supplies the search terms.
Share this: write three explanations for one ambiguous message before responding.

title: The Silver Tongue
question: A lecturer speaks fluently and uses beautiful slides, so students assume his historical claims are accurate. Which check most cleanly separates presentation quality from factual reliability?
choices: Compare his speaking confidence with other popular lecturers
Verify a preselected sample of claims against independent sources
Ask students how inspired they felt immediately after the lecture
Inspect whether his slides use consistent fonts and citations
correctAnswer: Verify a preselected sample of claims against independent sources
correctExplanation: Right. Independent fact-checking evaluates accuracy directly, whereas fluency and polish can create a halo without improving truth.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — verify a preselected sample of claims against independent sources. Inspiration, confidence, and visual consistency all belong to the presentation halo; sampling claims tests the separate trait at issue.
lessonContent:
Processing fluency makes information feel truer and its source feel more competent.
Style and substance can correlate, but one does not prove the other.
Preselecting claims prevents a checker from choosing only easy or favourable examples.
Independent sources break the loop in which polish validates itself.
Share this: fact-check one polished claim that you accepted mainly because it sounded smooth.

title: The Hidden Errors
question: A trainee labels medical images and says she is 95% accurate. She has never seen expert labels and cannot describe common error patterns. What feedback would most improve both skill and self-assessment?
choices: Praise her confidence so difficult cases feel less intimidating
Let her repeat only the images she already labelled quickly
Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses
Ask her to increase her confidence estimate after every completed set
correctAnswer: Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses
correctExplanation: Exactly. Item-level correction teaches the distinctions required both to perform well and to recognize one's own mistakes.
incorrectExplanation: Close! Compare each prediction with expert labels and explain near misses. Repetition without an answer key can automate errors; diagnostic feedback builds the knowledge that accurate self-grading requires.
lessonContent:
Poor calibration persists when learners receive completion signals but no correctness signals.
Detailed feedback teaches both task rules and the boundaries of current skill.
Near misses are valuable because they reveal which distinctions remain blurred.
Confidence should be scored against outcomes, not rewarded for its own intensity.
Share this: seek item-level feedback on one task you currently judge only by feel.

title: The Winning Metric
question: A team expects its redesign to help. After launch, retention falls but time-on-page rises, so it declares time-on-page the real goal. What would have best protected the evaluation from this shift?
choices: Collecting many more metrics after seeing the initial results
Letting the design team explain why its preferred metric matters
Removing any measure that contradicts the redesign's intended story
Committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds
correctAnswer: Committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds
correctExplanation: Correct. Advance commitments prevent the team from promoting whichever outcome happens to confirm its hope.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is committing beforehand to primary measures and decision thresholds. More metrics create more chances to find a flattering result; a preregistered rule separates prediction from post-hoc storytelling.
lessonContent:
When many outcomes are available, almost any result can support a preferred story.
Choosing success criteria after results converts testing into rationalization.
Advance commitments preserve the difference between prediction and explanation.
Secondary measures remain useful when clearly labelled as exploratory.
Share this: define success and failure before starting your next personal experiment.

title: Charisma at Scale
question: Investors love a founder's confidence and compelling mission, then rate the startup's security, market demand, and financial controls highly without checking them. Which process offers the strongest defence?
choices: Score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder
Invite the founder to give a longer and more detailed presentation
Average every investor's overall impression after the pitch
Treat confidence as evidence that hidden operational details are sound
correctAnswer: Score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder
correctExplanation: Exactly. Independent, pre-pitch risk scoring prevents personal magnetism from becoming evidence about controls the investors have not examined.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, score predefined evidence for each risk before meeting the founder. Longer exposure and averaged impressions can spread the same halo across the group; predefined criteria make each risk answer to its own evidence.
lessonContent:
Charisma is vivid social information that can contaminate technical judgements.
Group discussion does not cancel a halo when everyone shares the same first impression.
Predefined criteria reduce the freedom to reinterpret missing evidence favourably.
Evaluating components before the whole protects analysis from global liking.
Share this: make a scorecard before the next persuasive pitch you hear.

title: Calibration Class
question: The weakest performers in a statistics course greatly overrate their scores. After training, their scores and self-estimates both improve. What is the most careful interpretation?
choices: Their original confidence must have caused their weak performance
Learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work
Low performers always become less confident as soon as they practise
Accurate self-assessment develops independently of task knowledge
correctAnswer: Learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work
correctExplanation: Right. The knowledge that improves performance can also reveal what counts as an error, so skill and calibration may rise together.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — learning the subject also improved the tools needed to judge their work. The result does not show that confidence caused low scores or that confidence must fall; it shows task knowledge can support metacognition.
lessonContent:
Self-evaluation is not a separate magic faculty; it draws on domain knowledge.
Training can improve both answers and recognition of what a good answer requires.
Calibration means matching confidence to accuracy, not merely lowering confidence.
A learner may become more confident and better calibrated at the same time.
Share this: compare confidence and accuracy before and after your next study session.

title: The Referral Note
question: Before examining a patient, a doctor reads a referral strongly suggesting migraine. Every later symptom gets interpreted through that diagnosis. Which procedure best reduces the pull of the initial theory?
choices: Read the referral repeatedly until its reasoning is fully memorable
Ask the patient only questions that distinguish migraine subtypes
Record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral
Search old migraine cases for symptoms resembling this patient's report
correctAnswer: Record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral
correctExplanation: Exactly. An independent assessment preserves alternatives before the referral hypothesis can organize attention and interpretation.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to record an independent differential from raw findings before viewing the referral. Repeated referral review and migraine-focused questions narrow the search further; temporal separation protects a second evidential path.
lessonContent:
Diagnostic labels guide attention toward matching symptoms and away from alternatives.
Independent first-pass judgements preserve information that an anchor might suppress.
Differential reasoning keeps multiple causes alive until evidence separates them.
Order matters: evidence seen first can organize everything interpreted later.
Share this: form your own estimate before reading someone else's confident conclusion.

title: Prestige on Paper
question: Reviewers praise a candidate's writing, teamwork, and judgement after noticing she worked at a famous company. Which change most directly tests whether prestige is inflating unrelated ratings?
choices: Tell reviewers which famous teams the candidate collaborated with
Ask the candidate to describe why the company hired her
Have reviewers discuss the company's reputation before scoring
Remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently
correctAnswer: Remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently
correctExplanation: Correct. A blinded rescore changes the prestige cue while holding the underlying evidence constant.
incorrectExplanation: It's simpler than it looks: remove employer identities and rescore the same evidence independently. More discussion of the famous employer magnifies the halo; blinding creates a direct comparison of ratings with and without it.
lessonContent:
Institutional prestige can act as a halo around an individual's unmeasured qualities.
A clean test changes the identity cue while preserving the work being judged.
Independent rescoring prevents discussion from pressuring reviewers toward consensus.
Blind review cannot remove every bias, but it can isolate a specific source.
Share this: evaluate one piece of work before learning who made it.

title: Confident but Vague
question: In meetings, Arun confidently claims a project is 'certain to succeed' but gives no measurable forecast. Which request would make his self-assessment easiest to calibrate?
choices: Ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level
Ask him to repeat the claim after the team lists its concerns
Let him define success only after the project has finished
Count how many colleagues describe his delivery as convincing
correctAnswer: Ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level
correctExplanation: Exactly. A specific forecast can be scored later, turning impressive certainty into evidence about actual calibration.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to ask for a dated, testable prediction with a numerical confidence level. Vague certainty escapes correction because success can be redefined; scored forecasts reveal whether confidence frequencies match outcomes.
lessonContent:
Vague claims protect confidence from contact with failure.
Calibration compares stated probabilities with long-run outcome frequencies.
Dated forecasts prevent memory from polishing what was originally predicted.
Specificity turns confidence from a performance into a measurable claim.
Share this: attach a probability and deadline to one prediction you make today.

title: The Beloved Stock
question: An investor owns a company she admires. She reads every positive report and dismisses bad news as short-term noise. Which rule would best expose her thesis to genuine revision?
choices: Buy more whenever a favourable report confirms management's story
Write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates
Follow additional commentators who already own the same company
Judge each negative report by how uncomfortable it makes her feel
correctAnswer: Write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates
correctExplanation: Right. Advance exit criteria stop affection from moving the evidential goalposts whenever contrary information arrives.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — write observable sell conditions now and review them on fixed dates. More like-minded commentary compounds selective exposure; predetermined conditions state what evidence must trigger revision before emotions negotiate exceptions.
lessonContent:
Commitment makes disconfirming evidence easier to reinterpret as temporary noise.
A belief needs explicit revision conditions before contrary facts arrive.
Fixed review dates reduce reactions to daily emotional swings.
Decision rules are useful only when written clearly enough to resist later editing.
Share this: write one concrete condition that would make you abandon a current plan.

title: Warmth and Trust
question: A friendly contractor remembers everyone's names and apologizes charmingly for delays. The client therefore assumes his invoices are accurate. What evidence should carry the most weight?
choices: How sincerely he appears to regret each scheduling problem
How many clients describe him as pleasant to work with
Whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work
Whether his friendliness remains consistent during the audit
correctAnswer: Whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work
correctExplanation: Exactly. Warmth may matter for the relationship, but invoice accuracy is a separate claim requiring transactional evidence.
incorrectExplanation: Actually, check whether sampled charges match receipts, rates, and completed work. Charm and sincere apologies can cast a halo over honesty; matching records directly tests the financial claim.
lessonContent:
Warmth and integrity are distinct traits even when they often travel together.
Social ease can lower scrutiny precisely when verification still matters.
Sampling records tests a concrete claim without requiring global distrust.
Separating person-liking from process-checking protects both relationships and decisions.
Share this: verify one practical detail independently even when you like the person responsible.

title: The Narrow Certificate
question: After passing a short quiz on privacy rules, a manager claims she can design the company's entire data-governance system. What is the fairest way to assess that leap?
choices: Accept it because any formal certificate proves broad competence
Reject it because beginners can never assess their own progress
Repeat the same quiz until her score becomes nearly perfect
Test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks
correctAnswer: Test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks
correctExplanation: Correct. The quiz supports only the skill it sampled; broader competence must be demonstrated on broader tasks.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to test the additional skills with realistic, independently scored tasks. A narrow credential can trigger overgeneralization, but automatic rejection is also unjustified; representative evidence should decide.
lessonContent:
A test supports claims only about the knowledge and tasks it actually samples.
Beginners may overgeneralize a visible milestone into mastery of a wider system.
Representative tasks reveal planning, transfer, and error detection that quizzes can miss.
Fair calibration neither flatters nor dismisses; it measures the claimed scope.
Share this: state exactly what one of your credentials demonstrates and what it does not.

title: The Silent Estimates
question: A team lead predicts a two-week delivery and opens discussion by defending that estimate. Soon everyone finds reasons it is realistic. Which meeting change best preserves independent evidence?
choices: Collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view
Let the lead present more success stories before inviting objections
Ask only people who agree to explain their reasoning in detail
Take a public vote immediately after the lead's opening argument
correctAnswer: Collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view
correctExplanation: Exactly. Independent estimates prevent the leader's hypothesis from determining what everyone searches for and reports.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — collect private estimates and failure reasons before revealing anyone's view. Public discussion after an authoritative opening encourages supportive search and social alignment; simultaneous private input preserves diverse information.
lessonContent:
A stated group preference becomes a search cue for reasons that support it.
Independent elicitation protects information held by quieter or lower-status members.
Failure prompts counter the natural tendency to plan from the success story alone.
Reveal order matters because early views shape later evidence production.
Share this: gather written opinions before discussion at your next group decision.
